title: Convergence monitoring of quantum Gibbs samplers
authors: Nikolaos Louloudis, Ruben Ibarrondo, Mikel Sanz, Mario Berta
abstract: Recent progress in fully quantum Markov chain Monte Carlo methods enables efficient Gibbs-state sampling on quantum computers [Chen et al., Nature 646, 561 (2025)]. Although rigorous worst-case bounds on mixing times remain largely inaccessible for classically intractable systems, experience from classical Monte Carlo suggests that convergence of relevant observables may nevertheless be rapid. This raises the practical question of how to diagnose convergence efficiently, i.e., with at most polynomial overhead. We propose a low-cost criterion for convergence monitoring that exploits the weak measurements inherent in quantum Gibbs samplers and their qubit-efficient variants [Ding et al., arXiv:2508.05703 (2025)]. Our approach is based on the observation that, at thermal equilibrium, the net energy flow between system and environment vanishes and energy-exchange statistics satisfy a balance condition. This condition appears in the distribution of (quasi-)frequencies extracted from the weak-measurement record and we use it to construct a Hamiltonian-agnostic stopping criterion based solely on data already generated by the sampler. We provide a statistical analysis, along with numerical and analytical studies to understand its performance, assumptions, and limitations.
summary: The paper introduces a novel, low-cost method to monitor the convergence of Quantum Gibbs Samplers (QGSs) used for sampling thermal equilibrium states. It achieves this by monitoring an energy balance condition derived from weak measurement records inherent to the QGS process. This diagnostic tool allows researchers to determine when simulations have reached equilibrium without needing costly auxiliary measurements.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an efficient, low-cost method to diagnose when a quantum Gibbs sampler (QGS) has converged to the true thermal equilibrium state.
main_result: A Hamiltonian-agnostic stopping criterion is proposed that monitors energy flow balance conditions derived from weak measurements inherent in the QGS process. This allows for convergence diagnosis using only data already generated by the simulation.
method: The method exploits the physical requirement that net energy flow vanishes at equilibrium, translating this into a statistical test on the distribution of quasi-frequencies extracted from weak measurements.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum state evolving towards the Gibbs state $\rho_\beta = e^{-\beta H} / \text{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$ using Quantum Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods (QGSs). The process simulates open-system dynamics via Lindbladians.
key_observables: The mean and third centered moment of the weak-measurement record, which are used to construct a confidence ellipsoid for monitoring convergence.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature $\beta$, frequency resolution parameter $\sigma_E$, and tolerance parameters $P_j$ defining acceptable deviations from equilibrium constraints.
main_assumptions: The criterion is a practical diagnostic, not a worst-case guarantee, relying on the underlying structure of energy flow conservation and detailed balance conditions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the symmetry of transition weights at equilibrium versus asymmetry away from it. Figure 2 details the circuit implementation of Lindbladian simulation via weak measurement.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, proposes the energy-flow based criterion using weak measurements, provides statistical analysis and numerical studies to validate its performance, and discusses limitations regarding worst-case guarantees.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for theoretical physicists working on open quantum systems or many-body dynamics as it provides a practical tool to verify convergence in complex, non-equilibrium simulations without requiring auxiliary measurements.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Davies limit intuition for the convergence monitor- ing scheme. Weak system–bath coupling induces transitions labeled by Bohr frequencies ν. These transitions are inferred from the bath without directly measuring the system. At thermal equilibrium, detailed balance implies symmetry of the equilibrium transition weights, M(ν) = M(−ν), so the transition profile is symmetric about ν = 0. Away from equi- librium an asymmetric profile signals a residual imbalance in the energy-exchange record. The algorithmic sampler of Sec. There are two cases. If q′ = 0, all ancillas are reset and the system remains in ρ. If q′ = 1, the Lindbla- dian step is applied to S, and, conditioned on B = q = 0 the registers A and E return to a and ω, respectively; otherwise, the step is discarded.

Figure 3. Relation between the deterministic target distance DΛ,c(t) and the energy error εE,c(t) under deterministic Lindblad evolution. Rows correspond to the nearest-neighbour and fully connected Ising families, and columns to β ∈{0.5, 1.0, 1.5}. Marker shape distinguishes n ∈{3, 5, 7}, and color gives the physical Lindblad time. The legends report the actual terminal time tmax for each system size. The equilibration time increase with n and β and is also larger for the fully connected model. In all cases, we observe a co-decay which confirms that the quasi-frequency distribution can monitor the relaxation of the energy observable.

Figure 4. Inverse-temperature dependence of the deterministic energy-relaxation time Oc and the model-calibrated mean stopping time eSc of the ellipsoidal inclusion rule. Rows correspond to the two model families and columns to n ∈{3, 5, 7}. Error bars are 95% Student-t confidence intervals for the mean over 100 independent trajectories. The deterministic reference carries no trajectory-sampling error bar. A base-two logarithmic vertical axis is used. We see that the scaling of eSc has the same qualitative behavior as the offline oracle Oc.

Figure 5. Naive convergence monitoring by repeated state preparation and destructive measurement. The black curve represents the relaxation of an observable (for simplicity exponential), the vertical dashed lines denote monitoring times, and tmix marks the unknown time at which the selected convergence tolerance is attained.
